- Model consistently overestimates early in the 30-day horizon, especially in the first 5–7 days, then underestimates later — suggest adjusting forecast slope downward after initial spike.
- When sentiment is neutral (all 0.00), model tends to ignore downward momentum; if true outcome shows sharp drop, model should reduce forecast early.
- After a spike in price (e.g., 40.27 → 42.84), model overshoots and fails to correct — apply “overshoot decay” rule: reduce forecast by 1–2% per subsequent day after peak.
- Mean reversion is weak in early days but stronger in late horizon — model should allow 3–5% downward drift in final 5–7 days if no new sentiment triggers.
- If true outcome shows a strong upward trend (e.g., 37.17 → 42.84), model often fails to capture it — increase forecast sensitivity to recent low-to-high transitions, especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.
- Model underestimates true outcome when recent history includes a sharp drop (e.g., 40.27 → 37.17) — adjust forecast downward by 0.5–1.5% per day if sentiment remains flat.
- If sentiment history is all 0.00, model should not assume sentiment-driven momentum — treat as “no sentiment bias” and apply conservative correction.
